Class Compatibility

java.lang.Object
org.apache.openjpa.conf.Compatibility
public class Compatibility extends Object
Struct encompassing backwards-compatibility options.

    • getFlushBeforeDetach

      public boolean getFlushBeforeDetach()
      Whether OpenJPA should flush changes before detaching or serializing an entity. In JPA this is usually false, but other persistence frameworks (ie JDO) may expect it to be true.

      Prior to version 1.0.3 and 1.2.0 changes were always flushed.

      Returns:
      true if changes should be flushed, otherwise false.
      Since:
      1.0.3, 1.2.0

    • setIgnoreDetachedStateFieldForProxySerialization

      public void setIgnoreDetachedStateFieldForProxySerialization(boolean ignoreDSF)
      Whether OpenJPA should ignore the DetachedStateField value when determining if our Proxy classes should be removed during serialization.

      Starting with version 2.0.0, when the DetachedStateFiled==true, the build time $proxy classes will not be removed.

      Prior to version 2.0.0, the DetachedStateFiled was not used and the $proxy classes were not being removed during serialization after the Persistence context was cleared.

      Parameters:
      ignoreDSF - if true the old Proxy serialization behavior will be used.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • getIgnoreDetachedStateFieldForProxySerialization

      public boolean getIgnoreDetachedStateFieldForProxySerialization()
      Whether OpenJPA should ignore the DetachedStateField value when determining if our Proxy classes should be removed during serialization.

      Starting with version 2.0.0, when the DetachedStateFiled==true, the build time $proxy classes will not be removed.

      Prior to version 2.0.0, the DetachedStateFiled was not used and the $proxy classes were not being removed during serialization after the Persistence context was cleared.

      Returns:
      true if the old Proxy serialization will be used, otherwise false.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • getCopyOnDetach

      public boolean getCopyOnDetach()
      Affirms if detached entities are copy of the managed instances. Before this option is introduced, detached entities were by default copies of the managed entities unless the entire cache is detached, only then the detachment was in-place. This option changes the default behavior such that detachment is now in-place by default. To emulate the previous copy-on-detach behavior set this option to true. If the entire cache is being detached (when the persistence context is closed, for example), the detachement
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • setCopyOnDetach

      public void setCopyOnDetach(boolean copyOnDetach)
      Sets if detached entities are copy of the managed instances. Before this option is introduced, detached entities were by default copies of the managed entities unless the entire cache is detached, only then the detachment was in-place. This option changes the default behavior such that detachment is now in-place by default. To emulate the previous copy-on-detach behavior set this option to true.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • getResetFlushFlagForCascadePersist

      public boolean getResetFlushFlagForCascadePersist()
      Whether OpenJPA should reset the internal state (flush flag) when cascading a persist to another Entity. That is, when a flush is performed, OpenJPA keep state to indicate the flush has been performed. In certain cascade persist scenarios the fact that a flush has been performed prior to a cascade persist can cause certain entities to not be written to the database given the prior flush. This property, when set, will cause the flush flag to be reset in cascade scenarios. For more details see JIRA OPENJPA-2051

    • getCleanupOwnedTablesOnBulkDelete

      public boolean getCleanupOwnedTablesOnBulkDelete()
      Whether a bulk delete removes the rows of the join tables and element collection tables owned by the deleted entities. A bulk delete never cascades to related entities, but the rows of the tables owned by a deleted entity are not entities themselves and would dangle on deleted primary keys otherwise. Defaults to true; set to false to leave those rows behind. A candidate that owns a bi-directional join table then has to be deleted in memory, because the SQL bulk delete cannot maintain that table; the in-memory path loads the matching instances and deletes them one row at a time rather than with a single bulk statement.

      A delete without any criteria empties the owned tables outright. A filtered delete materializes the primary keys of the matching candidates first and deletes by those keys, so it holds them in memory, spends a configured query timeout per statement rather than per operation, and evaluates the criteria in a statement of its own.

      Since:
      4.2.0

    • setCleanupOwnedTablesOnBulkDelete

      public void setCleanupOwnedTablesOnBulkDelete(boolean b)
      Whether a bulk delete removes the rows of the join tables and element collection tables owned by the deleted entities.
      Since:
      4.2.0

    • getFlushAfterInMemoryBulkOperation

      public boolean getFlushAfterInMemoryBulkOperation()
      Whether a bulk update or delete that has to be executed in memory flushes the persistence context afterwards. The in-memory path applies the operation to the managed instances rather than to the database, so without the flush executeUpdate() reports a row count that no statement has carried to the database yet, and the operation is lost altogether if the context is cleared before it is committed. Defaults to true.

      The flush is not restricted to the affected instances - the kernel only flushes the whole transactional cache - so unrelated pending changes of the same context are written as well. Jakarta Persistence 3.1 section 4.10 states that "the persistence context is not synchronized with the result of the bulk update or delete", so neither flushing nor not flushing is mandated; set this to false to restore the 4.1.x timing, in which nothing is written until the next flush or commit. Suppressing the flush does not suppress the operation itself: the matching instances are still modified or marked for deletion in the persistence context and are written by the next flush or at commit.

      The flush also decides when the lifecycle callbacks of the affected instances run: @PostRemove and @PostUpdate (AFTER_DELETE_PERFORMED and AFTER_UPDATE_PERFORMED) fire during a flush, so they run inside executeUpdate() by default and at the next flush or at commit when this is false.

      The flush after the operation is skipped regardless of this setting when the runtime cannot flush incrementally, that is when OpenJPAConfiguration.OPTION_INC_FLUSH is not supported or a savepoint is set that the configured SavepointManager cannot flush incrementally. The behaviour is then the same as with this option turned off. This covers the flush after the operation only: the flush before the candidate query is not guarded against a savepoint, so an operation issued with pending changes and a savepoint set still fails.

      Since:
      4.2.0

    • setFlushAfterInMemoryBulkOperation

      public void setFlushAfterInMemoryBulkOperation(boolean b)
      Whether a bulk update or delete that has to be executed in memory flushes the persistence context afterwards.
      Since:
      4.2.0

    • getMapAutoApplyConvertedFields

      public boolean getMapAutoApplyConvertedFields()
      Whether an attribute without a mapping annotation of its own whose type is not serializable is mapped as a basic attribute when an auto-apply converter (@Converter(autoApply = true)) is registered for its type. Defaults to true, as Jakarta Persistence 3.2 section 3.9 requires: a converted attribute is a basic attribute, and an auto-apply converter applies to all attributes of its target type. The attribute is stored in a column of the converter's database type.

      Set to false to restore the OpenJPA 4.1.x mapping, in which such an attribute had no persistence strategy and was left out of the mapping with only a warning, so that its value was not stored. Attributes of a serializable type and attributes annotated with @Basic are not affected by this option.

      The enhancer decides which fields of a class are persistent, so the option has to be set where the enhancer sees it as well, e.g. in persistence.xml, and build-time enhanced classes have to be enhanced again after it changes. A class enhanced with the default keeps such an attribute persistent when the option is set to false at runtime only.

      Since:
      4.2.0

    • setMapAutoApplyConvertedFields

      public void setMapAutoApplyConvertedFields(boolean b)
      Whether an attribute whose type is not serializable is mapped as a basic attribute when an auto-apply converter is registered for its type.
      Since:
      4.2.0

    • getEmulateNativeSequences

      public boolean getEmulateNativeSequences()
      Whether a named generator that asks for a database sequence is backed by a table sequence when the database has no sequence objects at all, i.e. when the dictionary defines no NextSequenceQuery. Defaults to true. Set to false to get the historical behaviour, where such a generator fails to configure with "Your database dictionary does not support native sequences".

      The substitution keys the emulated sequence by the sequence name, so entities sharing one generator share one counter, and initialValue and allocationSize are honoured either way. It changes which object holds the identifier state, however: a schema built by an earlier OpenJPA release does not have the sequence table, and an application that generated identifiers elsewhere - a sequence created by hand plus an explicit NextSequenceQuery, for instance - should configure that query rather than rely on the fallback.

      Since:
      4.2.0

    • setEmulateNativeSequences

      public void setEmulateNativeSequences(boolean b)
      Whether a named generator that asks for a database sequence is backed by a table sequence when the database has no sequence objects at all.
      Since:
      4.2.0

    • getResolveConverterTypeHierarchy

      public boolean getResolveConverterTypeHierarchy()
      Whether the type arguments of an AttributeConverter<X, Y> are resolved through the whole type hierarchy of the converter class. Defaults to true: a converter that gets its attribute type X or its database type Y from a generic superclass, such as Base<X, Y> implements AttributeConverter<X, Y>, or from an interface that extends AttributeConverter maps its attribute to a column of the database type, and such a converter, like one whose attribute type is parameterized, is registered when it is declared autoApply.

      Set to false to restore the OpenJPA 4.1.x mapping for attributes whose converter declares its types through a generic superclass or interface: only a class in the superclass chain of the converter that implements AttributeConverter directly with concrete type arguments is considered, so such a serializable attribute is mapped as a serialized object (a BLOB, BYTEA on PostgreSQL) as in 4.1.x, and an autoApply converter of that kind or of a parameterized attribute type is not applied, as 4.1.x ignored autoApply. Converters that implement AttributeConverter directly with concrete type arguments are not affected by this option.

      Since:
      4.2.0

      public void setResolveConverterTypeHierarchy(boolean b)
      Whether the type arguments of an AttributeConverter are resolved through the whole type hierarchy of the converter class.
      Since:
      4.2.0
